5	Answer semantics:
6	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
7	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
8	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
9	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.
10	- Items with asOfStage set must be answered using only evidence whose stage is at or before that stage.

14	CASE OD2-DEV2-NOCONC (NOCONC, cross-domain): Calderbridge night-rota pilot: falls rise at two care homes
15	Setting: Larchmere Care Group runs nine residential care homes. Two homes in the town of Calderbridge, Ashby Fold (52 beds, two floors) and Penmor Lodge (44 beds, two floors), have piloted a reduced night-staffing rota since 1 June 2026. Group rollout of the rota to the other seven homes is planned for March 2027. You are the group quality lead, writing in mid-October 2026.
16	Presenting request: The Director of Operations wants a recommendation for the 12 November 2026 board. Should the group put Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge back on four night staff and halt the March 2027 rollout of the pilot rota? What explains the rise in recorded falls at the two homes?
17	INITIAL EVIDENCE
18	E1 [stage S1] Email from Marian Telfer, Director of Operations, to the group quality lead, 6 October 2026 (leadership-account): Subject: Calderbridge falls - board recommendation. Falls at our two night-rota pilot homes have nearly doubled: 16 in Q2, 31 in Q3 (Ashby Fold 9 to 17, Penmor Lodge 7 to 14). Since 1 June both homes have run nights with three staff (one carer per floor plus a floating senior) instead of four (two carers per floor). That is the obvious change. Night staff tell me they can't get to call bells as fast. We have no call-bell timings from before June, but I believe them. I want a recommendation for the 12 November board: put both homes back on four night staff now and pull the March rollout to the other seven homes. I am not prepared to wait another quarter.
19	E2 [stage S1] Group quality dashboard extract, Q3 2026, falls section (system-record): Recorded falls, Q2 to Q3 2026: Ashby Fold 9 to 17 (RED); Penmor Lodge 7 to 14 (RED); Brackenhill 11 to 9; Cresswell Court 8 to 9; Dunmore House 14 to 12; Elmstead 6 to 7; Fairholme 10 to 11; Greywater 12 to 9; Hatherley View 7 to 8. Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge combined, by month: Apr 4, May 5, Jun 7, Jul 11, Aug 9, Sep 11. RAG rule: red where the quarter-on-quarter rise exceeds 25%. Notes: figures are raw counts, not adjusted for occupancy. From 1 July, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge incidents are imported directly from the Tallyline incident app. All other homes' figures are keyed in from paper incident forms by site administrators.
20	E3 [stage S1] Interview notes, night senior carers at Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, 2-3 October 2026 (taken by the deputy quality lead) (staff-account): Ashby Fold night senior (9 years in post): 'With one carer per floor, if two bells go at once on the same floor somebody waits. We're slower, I'm sure of it, though I couldn't give you minutes.' Penmor Lodge night senior (in the floating role since June): 'It's different, not worse. Because I float, I'm usually free for the second bell. A lot of what's on the system now is people found sitting on the floor at the two o'clock check with no injury. We always had those. Whether they all got written up before, I honestly couldn't say.'
21	E4 [stage S1] Incident system query: falls by time of day, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge combined, Q2 and Q3 2026 (system-record): Night (22:00-07:00): Q2 8, Q3 18. Day (07:00-22:00): Q2 8, Q3 13. Night share of falls: Q2 50%, Q3 58%. Day staffing at both homes did not change during either quarter. Source note: Q2 times come from paper forms. The time field was blank on 3 forms, and the administrator assigned those from the shift recorded. Q3 times are stamped automatically by Tallyline when the entry is made, which may be some time after the fall was discovered.
22	E5 [stage S1] Replies from the two registered managers to the Director of Operations, 7 October 2026 (manager-account): Penmor Lodge manager: 'I don't think it's the rota. Since Hollin Street Medical Practice took over our residents in May, the new GPs have been reviewing everyone's medication, and some residents have been started on night-time tablets. I'd look there first.' Ashby Fold manager: 'We moved to Hollin Street in May as well. My worry is admissions. We've taken more people from the hospital discharge-to-assess beds this summer, and they arrive frailer than our usual referrals. The rota is tight, but I'm not convinced it's the whole story.'
23	CATALOGUE (full contents)
24	C1 [stage S1] Estates and maintenance log, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, April-September 2026 - Group estates helpdesk system (system-record): Ashby Fold: 14 jobs logged, including a boiler service (April), replacement of two failed first-floor corridor ceiling lights (July, completed the same day), an adjusted door closer on bedroom 12 (August) and garden path resurfacing (September). No flooring changes. Penmor Lodge: 11 jobs logged, including a lift inspection (May), a lounge carpet deep-clean (June), a replacement nurse-call handset in room 7 (July) and a kitchen extractor repair (September). No flooring or lighting changes in resident areas. Night lighting levels at both homes were last surveyed in 2025 and met the group standard.
25	C2 [stage S1] Monthly falls per 1,000 occupied bed days, all nine homes, January 2023-September 2026, with control limits - Group quality analyst, statistical chart pack (document): Analyst's summary (D. Raman, group quality analyst). Rates use occupied bed days. Three-sigma limits were set on January 2023-May 2026 data. Ashby Fold: long-run mean 2.6 falls per 1,000 bed days; quarterly rates since 2023 ranged from 1.8 to 3.9; Q2 2026 was 2.0, its second-lowest quarter; Q3 2026 was 3.7. Penmor Lodge: mean 2.9; range 1.9-4.1; Q2 2026 1.9, Q3 2026 3.7. No monthly point at either home is above its upper limit, and no run rule is triggered. Since 2023, single homes in the group have had five other quarter-on-quarter rises of 70% or more, and each fell back the next quarter without specific action. Caution: at these volumes, a real, sustained increase of around 40% would usually take two to three quarters to show as a signal, so points inside the limits do not show that nothing changed.
26	C3 [stage S1] Night agency and bank shift usage, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, April-September 2026 - Group workforce and finance system (financial-record): Share of night shifts filled by agency or bank staff: Ashby Fold 12% in Q2, 13% in Q3; Penmor Lodge 9% in Q2, 10% in Q3. The same three agencies were used throughout. All agency staff complete the group's falls and moving-and-handling induction before their first night shift. Night shifts that ran below rota: Ashby Fold 2 in Q2, 1 in Q3; Penmor Lodge 0 in Q2, 1 in Q3. The pilot cut the number of night shifts to fill by a quarter, so total night agency spend fell.
27	C4 [stage S1] Tallyline implementation briefing to the group, May 2026 - Tallyline customer success manager, slide notes (vendor-account): Slide notes: 'Most care providers see recorded incidents rise after go-live, often sharply and sometimes doubling, because staff can log an incident in under a minute at the point of care. This is a sign of a healthier reporting culture, not of more harm.' When asked for supporting data, the vendor referred to anonymised customer case studies. It did not provide figures, comparison groups or its definition of 'incident'. The briefing formed part of the group's contract negotiation for the January 2027 rollout to the remaining seven homes.
28	C5 [stage S1] Clinical governance monthly packs, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, April-September 2026 - Registered managers' monthly governance returns (system-record): Occupancy: Ashby Fold 94% (Q2), 95% (Q3); Penmor Lodge 93%, 94%. Admissions Q2/Q3: Ashby Fold 4/3, of which from discharge-to-assess beds 3/2; Penmor Lodge 3/3. Mean dependency score (1-4 scale): Ashby Fold 2.61 to 2.58; Penmor Lodge 2.70 to 2.74. Hollin Street medication reviews, May-September: 23 residents reviewed; 14 medicines stopped, 4 doses reduced, 2 started (a night-time hypnotic for one Penmor resident, who has had no recorded fall, and a statin). Residents on any psychotropic or hypnotic: Ashby Fold 21 to 20; Penmor Lodge 18 to 18. Falls by resident: 27 of the 31 Q3 falls, and 13 of the 16 Q2 falls, were by residents who lived at the homes throughout both quarters. Highest individual count: one Penmor resident, 4 in Q2 and 5 in Q3. Nobody else had more than 3 in either quarter.
29	C6 [stage S1] Nurse-call system export of night call response times, Ashby Fold, and nurse-call supplier note, Penmor Lodge - Nurse-call system export and supplier email (log): Ashby Fold: the system keeps 45 days of call data, so the earliest available record is 16 August. Night calls from 16 August to 30 September: 1,212. Median time to answer 3 min 40 s; 9% took more than 10 minutes. No pre-pilot data survive, and the group has no standard for night response time. Penmor Lodge: the nurse-call panel (installed 2014) records calls but not answer times. The supplier confirms that no response-time data can be extracted. Neither home's figures can be compared with the period before 1 June.
30	C7 [stage S1] Night staffing pilot protocol (approved April 2026) and status note, 3 October 2026 - Executive team papers (document): Purpose: test one carer per floor plus a floating senior at two homes before group rollout. Safeguards: each home's falls rate is reviewed monthly on the group control chart. The pilot pauses at a home if any month breaches the upper control limit, or if falls with harm (first aid or more) exceed 6 in a quarter at that home. Evaluation: the rollout decision is taken after at least two full quarters of data. Signed by the Director of Finance and the Director of Operations, with the Director of Operations' reservation about night cover recorded. Status note, 3 October: neither pause criterion has been met at either home.
31	C8 [stage S1] Falls-prevention and moving-and-handling training records, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, 2026 - Group learning management system (system-record): Mandatory falls-prevention e-learning compliance: Ashby Fold 88% (June), 90% (September); Penmor Lodge 91%, 92%. Practical moving-and-handling refresher in date: Ashby Fold 85%, 87%; Penmor Lodge 89%, 90%. The group target for both is 85%. At both homes, night-staff compliance is within two percentage points of day-staff compliance. The training content did not change in 2026.
32	C9 [stage S1] Tallyline go-live record, falls by harm level Q2-Q3 2026, and Q2 handover-note cross-check, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge - Deputy quality lead, compiled from Tallyline, paper forms and handover books (document): Go-live: 1 July 2026 at both homes, which were chosen to give the rota pilot better night data. Other homes are scheduled for January 2027. Falls by harm level, both homes combined, Q2 to Q3: no harm 10 to 22; first-aid harm 4 to 6; GP or hospital attendance 2 to 3. Unwitnessed 'found on floor' falls: 5 to 14. Handover cross-check (September): night handover notes for 6 of the 13 Q2 weeks were compared with the paper incident forms. These were the weeks whose notes could still be found. Three entries clearly describe an unreported fall, and three more are ambiguous ('sitting on floor, assisted up'). No equivalent Q3 check is possible because handover notes are now written inside Tallyline. The cross-check therefore cannot say how many falls Tallyline itself misses.
33	C10 [stage S1] Director of Operations' memo to the executive team on the proposed night staffing pilot, 18 March 2026 - Executive team papers (leadership-account): 'I do not support reducing night staff to save £410,000 a year across the group. Four on nights is the safe minimum for two-floor homes, and I expect falls to rise if we cut it. If the executive proceeds, I want it on record that I warned against this.' Minute, 2 April 2026: the executive approved a two-home pilot, and the Director of Operations' reservation was recorded.
34	C11 [stage S1] Family complaints and compliments log, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, April-September 2026 - Group customer relations log (system-record): Complaints: Ashby Fold 3 (May: lost laundry; May: call bell 'took ages' at night; August: relative not told promptly about a no-harm fall); Penmor Lodge 2 (June: visiting hours; September: menu choice). Compliments: Ashby Fold 7, Penmor Lodge 9. No complaint mentions staffing levels. The August complaint was resolved after the home showed the family the Tallyline record and the time they were notified.
35	C12 [stage S1] Post-fall observation completion audit, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, Q2 and Q3 2026 - Group clinical audit team (system-record): Group policy requires a 24-hour observation schedule (pulse, blood pressure and consciousness checks) after any unwitnessed fall or head strike. Full schedule completed: Q2 (paper prompts) 4 of 6 eligible falls, 67%; Q3 (Tallyline sends timed reminders for each logged fall) 15 of 16 eligible falls, 94%. One Q3 head injury was identified at the 4-hour check, and the resident was sent to hospital the same evening. The other seven homes, still on paper, averaged 62% in Q3.
36	C13 [stage S1] Anonymous night-staff pulse survey, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, September 2026 - Trade-union branch survey (14 of 22 night staff responded) (anonymous-staff-survey): 'Compared with before June, is your night workload...' Heavier 9, about the same 4, lighter 1. 'Do you now log incidents you would not have written up on paper?' Yes 8, no 4, not sure 2. Free-text examples: 'paper forms took 20 minutes, so the little ones went in the handover book'; 'the floating senior helps but she's always on the other floor when you need her'; 'Tallyline nags you until you've done the obs.' The union branch ran the survey, and the operations team helped draft the questions.
37	C14 [stage S1] Most recent regulator inspection reports, Ashby Fold (March 2025) and Penmor Lodge (October 2024) - Care regulator public reports (regulator-record): Ashby Fold: rated Good overall, with Good in the safe domain. Inspectors noted that 'falls risk assessments are in place and reviewed monthly; sensor equipment is used appropriately'. One recommendation: update fire evacuation plans. Penmor Lodge: rated Good overall. The safe domain was rated Requires Improvement because of medicines storage temperatures, which has since been resolved. No enforcement action at either home. Neither inspection looked at night staffing in detail.
38	C15 [stage S1] Infection-control and outbreak log, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, April-September 2026 - Group infection prevention lead (system-record): No outbreaks were declared at either home. Urinary tract infections treated: Ashby Fold 6 in Q2, 5 in Q3; Penmor Lodge 4 in Q2, 5 in Q3. Chest infections: Ashby Fold 2 and 1; Penmor Lodge 1 and 2. One Penmor Lodge resident tested positive for a respiratory virus in August and was isolated for five days, with no onward spread. Hydration charts were audited monthly at both homes, and no concerns were raised.
39	CANDIDATES
40	H1: The night-staffing pilot that began in June raised residents' underlying risk of falling at the two homes.
41	H2: The rise mainly reflects more complete recording of falls after the two homes switched to the incident app, rather than more falls actually happening.
42	H3: A shift in the resident population at the two homes toward frailer, higher-risk residents drove the rise.
43	H4: Underlying fall risk at the two homes did not change, and the Q3 figures are ordinary quarter-to-quarter variation for homes of this size.
44	H5: Prescribing changes made after the two homes moved to a new GP practice raised residents' fall risk.
45	R1: Night-staffing pilot at the two homes (one carer per floor plus a floating senior) -> Higher recorded fall counts at the two homes in Q3 2026 (increases)
46	R2: Switch from paper incident forms to the incident app at the two homes -> Higher recorded fall counts at the two homes in Q3 2026 (increases)
47	R3: Change in resident mix toward frailer admissions at the two homes -> Higher recorded fall counts at the two homes in Q3 2026 (increases)
48	R4: Night-staffing pilot at the two homes -> Slower answering of night call bells (increases)
49	A1: Return both homes to four night staff now and suspend the March rollout of the pilot rota to the other seven homes.
50	A2: Keep the pilot running under its existing pause criteria. Re-present falls as rates on the control chart with the change in reporting method marked, start manual sampling of night call-bell response times at both homes, and take the rollout decision at a dated review in late January using Q4 data.
51	A3: Issue formal capability warnings to the night senior carers at both homes over the rise in falls.
52	A4: Withdraw the incident app at the two homes and return them to paper forms until all nine homes can switch together, so that the dashboard compares like with like.
53	SCORED ITEMS
54	Q01: hypothesis H1 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
55	Q02: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
56	Q03: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
57	Q04: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
58	Q05: hypothesis H5 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
59	Q06: edge R1 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
60	Q07: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
61	Q08: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
62	Q09: edge R4 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
63	Q10: action A1 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
64	Q11: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
65	Q12: action A3 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
66	Q13: action A4 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
67	Q14: sufficiency SUFF allowed=[sufficient, insufficient]

answers.justification: The rise coincides with the pilot (E1, E2), and June was already up on paper forms before the app went live. However, the change in recording (C9, C13), the lack of before-and-after call-bell data (C6), conflicting staff accounts (E3) and a non-signal on the control chart (C2) mean the pilot effect is neither established nor ruled out.

Several things point to better recording: no-harm and found-on-floor falls rose most (C9), the Q2 handover notes show unreported falls (C9), and staff say they now log more (C13, E3). But the June rise came before the app went live (E2, C9), harmed falls also rose slightly, and the app's own miss rate is unknown (C9). So 'mainly' is not established.

C5 shows few admissions and fewer from discharge-to-assess beds at Ashby Fold, flat occupancy and dependency, and 27 of the 31 Q3 falls by long-stay residents. This contradicts the manager's claim in E5.

Both homes stay inside their control limits, and similar rises have reverted before (C2). But C2 warns that a real 40% rise would take two to three quarters to show, so the chart cannot confirm that nothing changed.

Per C5, the GP reviews mostly stopped or reduced medicines, the one hypnotic started went to a resident with no recorded fall, and psychotropic and hypnotic use was flat. This counts against the manager's claim in E5.
The pilot coincides in time and place with the rise: only the pilot homes went red (E2). But the app switch at the same homes is an uncontrolled rival (C9, C4), so causation is not established.

Recorded falls rose with the app switch, there is a plausible mechanism and some evidence of under-reporting on paper (C9, C13). But the June rise came first and the pilot is a concurrent rival (E2), so causation is not shown.
C5 shows no shift toward frailer admissions: discharge-to-assess admissions fell, dependency was flat, and most falls were by long-stay residents.

No pre-pilot response times exist at Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge records no answer times at all (C6). Staff accounts conflict (E3), and a slow-bell complaint was made in May, before the pilot (C11). So even an association cannot be shown.
Reverting would be justified if H1 were confirmed. But no pause criterion has been met (C7), the rise is confounded with the app switch (C9), and it is not a control-chart signal (C2).

A2 keeps the agreed safeguards (C7), corrects the dashboard's raw-count and reporting-method flaws (E2, C2, C9), fills the call-bell data gap (C6), and sets a dated decision point with Q4 data, which C2 says is needed to detect a real rise.

Nothing points to individual fault: training compliance is in date (C8), and better recording may itself explain the rise (C9, C13). Disciplining staff would punish the wrong party and discourage reporting.

The app raised completion of post-fall observations from 67% to 94% and caught a head injury (C12), and it captures falls that paper missed (C9). Withdrawing it would disable a protective control and suppress information.

The catalogue cannot separate the pilot effect from the recording change or chance (C2, C6, C9). The evidence therefore cannot support committing to a substantive decision now, either to revert or to proceed with rollout. A2's dated review exists for exactly that reason.

Unreported falls in the Q2 handover notes (3 clear and 3 ambiguous in 6 of 13 weeks, roughly 6-13 over the quarter if extrapolated), together with the rise concentrated in no-harm and found-on-floor falls, could account for most of the +15. Against that, the June paper-era rise and the rise in harmed falls argue for 'unknown'.

Q07: 'causal' is arguable, because there is a mechanism (paper forms took 20 minutes, so small falls went in the handover book) plus covariation plus direct evidence of Q2 under-reporting. But the pilot is a concurrent rival that has not been excluded.

Q14: it depends on whether A2 (continue the pilot plus a review) counts as a substantive decision. If keeping the pilot under its existing safeguards is treated as a substantive choice, 'sufficient' is defensible because it follows the pre-agreed protocol (C7).
Q06: 'unknown' is arguable if the confounded co-occurrence is not treated as showing an association attributable to the pilot.
caseProblems: E2/C9: the combined June count (7) already rose before the 1 July app go-live, on paper forms. This is a useful discriminating clue, but answer keys should check that it is intended, since it cuts against H2's 'mainly' claim.
C9 includes the phrase 'which were chosen to give the rota pilot better night data'. This openly explains why the two interventions were confounded, which is realistic but makes the confound salient.
C13: the operations team (aligned with the Director of Operations) helped draft the union survey questions. This is a deliberate bias marker that is fine, but worth noting.
C4: the vendor says the app rollout to the remaining homes is January 2027, consistent with C9. The pilot rota rollout is March 2027. No inconsistency, but readers could confuse the two rollouts.
Numeric checks pass: monthly, quarterly, time-of-day and harm-level totals reconcile (16 and 31), and the C2 rates match the occupancy figures in C5. No inconsistencies found.
No catalogue title leaks an answer outright. C12's title and content strongly signal that A4 is harmful, which is appropriate.
